title: Human papillomavirus vaccination coverage among adolescent girls and young women living with HIV in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis
content:
by Ifeyinwa Lilian Ezenwosu, John Olajide Olawepo, Jane Nnedinma Ohaekweiro, Peter Ezeogo Ihere, Emeka John Aneke, Justus Uchenna Onu, Oluchukwu Perpetual Okeke, Olajide Odunayo Sobande

Introduction

Human Papilloma Virus (HPV)-attributable cancers disproportionately affect adolescent girls and young women living with HIV (AGYWLHIV) in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet HPV vaccination coverage in this subpopulation remains suboptimal. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV in LMICs.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), and Web of Science for observational studies published between January 2014 and December 2025. A random-effects meta-analysis was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of HPV vaccination coverage. Subgroup analyses by age group and vaccine type were conducted, while HPV vaccination delivery platforms were summarised descriptively. Publication bias and sensitivity analyses were also performed, and statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using the I² statistic.

Results

A total of 8 studies involving 1,059 AGYWLHIV were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV in LMICs was 28.6% (95% CI: 20.3%–38.7%) based on a random-effects model, with substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 87.0%, p < 0.0001). Exploratory subgroup analysis by age yielded HPV vaccination coverage of 90.3% (95% CI: 74.2%–98.0%) among participants aged 9–14 years (1 study; n = 31) and 19.2% (95% CI: 11.0%–31.4%) among those aged 15–26 years (4 studies; n = 250). Exploratory descriptive findings indicated that HPV vaccination was delivered through health facilities, schools, community outreach, and combinations of these approaches. However, differences in denominators limited direct comparisons between delivery platforms.

Conclusion

The available evidence from studies conducted in LMICs indicates low HPV vaccination coverage among AGYWLHIV. Integrating HPV vaccination into routine HIV care may represent a potentially useful strategy to improve access and reduce missed vaccination opportunities among AGYWLHIV and should be further evaluated alongside broader efforts supported by strong political commitment and multisectoral collaboration.
